title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across both arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report every paired episode as safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared candidate per task passed deterministic validation in every case and no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked; this mechanistic fact explains the degenerate paired contrast. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, statistical mapping to archived outputs, an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation of operator intent to safe device configuration is central to modern NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce human‑readable configuration plans, but token‑level fidelity metrics fail to capture ordering, dependencies, and invariants that determine run‑time safety. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device emulators or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss. The generate–validate–repair (GVR) architecture (LLM generation + deterministic verification + automated repair) is widely proposed to mitigate such failures and has shown promise in program and configuration repair settings. However, it remains unclear under which experimental regimes a verifier produces an observable paired improvement in safety, especially under distribution shift and adversarial prompts.

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) that measured a single, precisely defined estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The study was executed in an emulation‑grounded benchmark environment with deterministic scoring. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of the preregistered paired GVR experiment and exact numeric outcomes; (2) an evidence‑based analysis explaining why the paired contrast was null under the chosen generation semantics; and (3) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to design future paired GVR evaluations that can produce informative discordant outcomes.
sections.related_work:
Emulation‑grounded benchmarks that place LLM agents in closed‑loop network configuration have recently been proposed to reveal workflow and planning faults beyond textual fidelity [1]. Prior work on automatic configuration and program repair documents GVR‑style patterns and shows that validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2], [4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for NetOps automation and safety [3], [5]. Engineering precedents from configuration analysis tools (for example, Batfish) provide incremental verification strategies applicable to verifier design [6].

Our study differs from prior work by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (explicitly preregistered), emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and archival of per‑call traces and validator traces so that every principal numeric claim is traceable to archived artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) computed on matched task pairs, where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis used a paired contingency approach, bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test for discordant pairs.

Design and task corpus: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial LLM generation per task is produced and reused across both arms; the guarded condition may invoke at most one validator‑triggered repair to produce a final guarded output. We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks grouped into 144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift (novel topology/vendor), and 48 adversarial‑prompt tasks. Tasks were generated deterministically from the benchmark task generator used by the emulation environment. The paired structure and shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered; under this contract only validator failures of the shared candidate or successful repairs can create discordant pairs.

Models, adapter, and oracle: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1). The guarded pipeline incorporated a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted up to one automated repair invocation per task. The adapter was configured to record per‑call metadata and to respect the shared_initial_candidate contract (one initial generation per task shared across arms).

Scoring, exclusions, missingness: Final safety was decided by deterministic emulator execution and invariant checks implemented by the validator. Preregistered exclusion rules removed pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe result) from the primary analysis and included them in sensitivity analyses; infra failures after prespecified retries were to be excluded from primary analysis and documented. The preregistered retry policy allowed limited infra retries; the execution manifest recorded all retry counts and failure tallies.

Statistical procedures: The primary analysis used a paired binary executor to produce the contingency table and the paired risk difference; bootstrap CIs used 10,000 resamples (seed recorded in archived analysis logs). Discordant‑pair testing used the exact McNemar two‑sided test. Secondary analyses included repair‑iteration counts and model‑call budgets per arm.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. The model‑call audit shows exactly one initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240 and model calls used = 240), consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions were recorded.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The observed counts are baseline safe = 240/240 and guarded safe = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Therefore the paired risk difference (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; archived seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were invoked in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0). Representative validator traces record validation checks, difficulty labels (for example, "very_hard" and "extreme"), parsed command counts, and final_state snapshots; in every case the shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation and thus remained the final configuration for both arms. Consequently, baseline and guarded final outputs were identical across all tasks and subgroups (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial), producing the degenerate paired outcome.

Planned but unused sensitivity channels: The preregistered sensitivity analyses for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures were not exercised because no flagged or infra‑failed pairs occurred. The planned subgroup paired contrasts are therefore degenerate (all zeros) in the archived analysis outputs.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one LLM output per task that both arms used. Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome by invoking a validator‑triggered repair when the shared candidate failed validation. Because the shared initial candidates passed deterministic validation in every episode, the guarded pipeline never invoked repair and hence could not produce discordant (guarded-only safe or baseline-only safe) outcomes. This execution‑level fact—adherence to shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with universal validator PASS—fully accounts for the observed paired contingency (n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0).

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and ensures direct pairing of generator outputs, but it constrains empirical causal contrast: verification can only affect outcomes when the single shared generator sample fails. To measure verifier benefit as a causal intervention, experimenters should consider one or more of the following modifications: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm so the guarded arm can exercise different generator draws that the validator may accept or reject; (B) increase adversary strength or diversify adversarial protocols to produce more generator failures that exercise the validator and repair logic; or (C) increase repair budget (permit multiple iterative repairs) so repair search is more likely to alter final configurations. Each approach targets a different causal pathway by which a validator can alter final applied configurations and generate informative discordant pairs.

Threats to validity: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract was an explicit preregistered choice that restricts causal interpretation; we preserve and disclose that design choice. Construct validity: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of semantic checks; passing that validator does not guarantee absence of all possible semantic faults in arbitrary production environments. External validity: the task corpus is emulation‑grounded and synthetic; extrapolation to large, heterogeneous production networks requires caution. Conclusion validity: observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 in this run prevented detection of a positive verifier effect under the chosen contract; future power planning should consider generator variability and adversary strength to ensure nondegenerate discordant counts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all 240 paired episodes were safe under both the LLM‑only baseline and the guarded GVR arm, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics made the paired contrast contingent on validator failures of the single shared candidate; because every shared candidate passed deterministic validation, no repairs were invoked and the paired contrast is degenerate. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support these conclusions and point to concrete experimental changes—generation semantics, adversary design, and repair budgeting—that are necessary for future paired GVR studies to produce informative discordant outcomes.

No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded benchmark; external validity to production, heterogeneous multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across other models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of semantic checks; passing the validator does not guarantee absence of all semantic faults in operational deployments.
